Abstract
Continuous keystroke dynamics authentication can strengthen password-based access control,
but its reliability can decline when legitimate typing behaviour changes because of fatigue,
device changes, stress, injury, and natural behavioural variation. The aim of this study was to
design, develop, and evaluate A Multilayered Model for Concept Drift Resilient Keystroke
Dynamics Authentication. The study followed a Design Science Research methodology
supported by quantitative experimental evaluation. The CMU DSL Keystroke Dynamics
Benchmark was used to develop the benchmark authentication model, while a controlled
synthetic stream was used to test drift monitoring and adaptation. The prototype used dwell-
time and flight-time features, profile-centred dwell and flight deltas, a class-balanced logistic
regression deployment model, a Streaming Random Patches stream model with Hoeffding Tree
learners, and ADWIN for drift detection. The deployed benchmark model achieved validation
accuracy of 0.9956, false acceptance rate of 0.0080, false rejection rate of 0.0000, and balanced
accuracy of 0.9960 under the defined protocol. The study contributes a reproducible data
science pipeline, a browser-based demonstration dashboard, and a model that links behavioural
biometric scoring with model-health monitoring and decision support.
Keywords: keystroke dynamics, continuous authentication, behavioural biometrics, concept
drift, stream mining, ADWIN, adaptive learning.

CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background of the Study
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology identifies reliable identity
verification and authentication as central components of digital identity management [1].
Conventional authentication, however, is commonly concentrated at session entry, which
motivates the collection of additional identity evidence during an active session [2], [3]. Breach
investigations further identify stolen or misused credentials as an important attack path [4].
These sources establish the need for post-login assurance without implying that login controls
are defective for performing their intended entry-point function.
Continuous authentication addresses this post-login assurance problem by collecting
behavioural evidence during an active session rather than relying solely on the entry-point login
decision [2], [3]. Keystroke dynamics has been applied to continuous authentication [2], while
continuous user authentication has been framed as an ongoing verification problem across
practical device environments [3]. Behavioural evidence can therefore complement a password
or public-key authenticator by indicating whether current interaction remains consistent with
the enrolled user.
Keystroke dynamics is the analysis of measurable timing patterns produced when a person
types. Software records key-press and key-release timestamps, from which features such as
dwell time and flight time are calculated. It does not capture the content of keyboard interaction
itself; rather, it measures how the user types, making it a passive behavioural biometric that
can be collected without specialised hardware [5], [6]. Identity verification using keystroke
latencies was demonstrated in early work [5], keystroke timing was subsequently treated as a
behavioural biometric [6], and dynamic keystroke analysis was shown to support identity
verification [7]. Later reviews show that performance depends strongly on feature
representation, task design, and evaluation protocol [8], [9], [10].
A central limitation is that typing behaviour is not stationary. Empirical work shows that
keystroke timing may vary with mental fatigue [11] and input device [12], while adaptive-
authentication research addresses behavioural change over time [13]. Concept-drift research
similarly shows that a learned relationship can lose validity when the data-generating context
changes [14], [15]. An unchanged keystroke model may therefore increase false rejections
when legitimate behaviour evolves, even if its initial benchmark accuracy was high.
13

Keystroke dynamics has been shown to support continuous verification [2], though practical
challenges persist across device environments [3]. Reported performance depends heavily on
feature representation and evaluation protocol [8]. Meanwhile, concept-drift research
establishes that models operating on changing data streams require active monitoring and
adaptation [15], and adaptive windowing offers a classifier-independent method for detecting
prediction-error drift [16]. However, these four functions classification, drift detection,
adaptation, and operational feedback are commonly evaluated in isolation rather than as an
integrated system. This study consequently examines whether they can be combined into a
single multilayered resilience model and evaluated through both a public benchmark protocol
and a controlled drift stream.
1.2 Problem Statement
Keystroke dynamics can support post-login behavioural verification because continuous-
authentication research shows that user identity can be checked during an active session rather
than only at login [2]. Continuous user-authentication research also shows that practical
systems must manage user variability, device conditions, privacy, and response latency [3].
Keystroke-latency studies demonstrate that timing patterns can distinguish users [5], while later
keystroke-dynamics work treats such timing as a behavioural biometric for authentication [6].
Dynamic keystroke-analysis research further supports identity verification using typing rhythm
[7]. However, keystroke behaviour is not permanently stable. Mental-fatigue research shows
that typing timing can change under fatigue [11], cross-device research shows that input
devices affect keystroke features [12], and adaptive-authentication work shows that
behavioural profiles may need updating over time [13]. Concept-drift theory explains that
learned models may lose reliability when the relationship between features and labels changes
[14], while later drift research emphasises monitoring and adaptation in changing data streams
[15]. Therefore, the problem addressed in this study is the limited evidence of an integrated,
reproducible keystroke-authentication model that combines profile-centred features,
authentication scoring, drift detection, adaptive response, and interpretable feedback.
1.3 Aim of the Study
The aim of this study was to develop a multilayered machine learning model for keystroke
dynamics authentication that is resilient to concept drift arising from natural changes in user
typing behaviour.
14

1.4 Research Objectives
The study pursued the following objectives:
1. To determine the discriminative power of profile-centred timing features in separating
genuine-user from impostor keystroke behaviour.
2. To develop a multilayered keystroke authentication model incorporating drift detection to
sustain authentication performance under concept drift.
3. To evaluate the multilayered keystroke authentication model's resilience to concept drift.
1.5 Research Questions
The research questions correspond directly with the objectives:
1. How effectively do profile-centred timing features separate genuine-user from impostor
keystroke behaviour?
2. How can drift detection be incorporated into a multilayered keystroke authentication model?
3. How resilient is the multilayered keystroke authentication model when concept drift is
introduced?
1.6 Significance of the Study
Researchers in behavioural biometrics benefit from a reproducible example of how static
keystroke classification can be evaluated together with model-health monitoring within a single
artifact. System developers benefit from an explicit architecture linking timing features,
authentication probability, threshold logic, drift detection, and model adaptation. University
and institutional security teams benefit from evidence about the opportunities and limitations
of adding keyboard-timing behaviour as a secondary assurance signal. Users benefit indirectly
from the study's emphasis on both false acceptance, which affects security, and false rejection,
which affects legitimate access.
1.7 Assumptions of the Study
The study assumed that the CMU fixed-text timing measurements contained sufficient user-
specific variation for controlled authentication analysis. It also assumed that a planned shift in
synthetic dwell and flight distributions could test the operation of the drift mechanism, while
recognising that synthetic change is not equivalent to longitudinal human behavioural drift.
1.8 Delimitations
Methodologically, the primary deployment experiment used a one-versus-rest protocol for
enrolled subject s036, while a secondary analysis repeated the protocol for all 51 CMU
15

subjects. The stream evaluation was limited to a deterministic synthetic sequence with an
abrupt change. Temporally, the study used existing benchmark sessions and a simulated stream
rather than collecting new longitudinal observations over months. Geographically, no claim is
made about a Zimbabwean or regional user population because the public benchmark was not
collected for that purpose. Technically, the study was restricted to desktop fixed-text timing,
dwell and flight features, logistic-regression deployment scoring, Streaming Random Patches
adaptation, and ADWIN error monitoring.
1.9 Definition of Key Terms
Continuous authentication: repeated verification of an active user using evidence collected
during a session.
Keystroke dynamics: behavioural biometric analysis of timing measurements derived from
key-press and key-release events.
Dwell time: the duration between pressing and releasing a key.
Flight time: the interval between releasing one key and pressing the next key.
Concept drift: change over time in the statistical relationship represented by a predictive model
[14], [15].
False Acceptance Rate (FAR): the proportion of impostor attempts incorrectly accepted.
False Rejection Rate (FRR): the proportion of genuine attempts incorrectly rejected.
1.10 Chapter Summary
This chapter established the post-login assurance problem from authentication, behavioural-
biometric, and concept-drift literature. It defined the study's response as a multilayered
resilience model that combines profile-centred keystroke classification with drift monitoring
and adaptive evaluation. The chapter also aligned three objectives with three research questions
and delimited the claims to a selected-subject benchmark protocol and controlled synthetic
drift. Chapter 2 examines the theories and prior studies that support this model.
16

CHAPTER 2: LITERATURE REVIEW
2.1 Introduction
This chapter develops the theoretical and empirical basis for the study. It first explains
Behavioural Biometrics Theory and Concept Drift Theory (Section 2.2) as the dual theoretical
pillars. It then reviews continuous authentication (2.3.1), keystroke dynamics as a behavioural
biometric (2.3.2), concept drift in authentication (2.3.3), and adaptive stream learning (2.3.4).
Subsequent sections examine drift detection methods (2.4), biometric performance evaluation
(2.5), and security, privacy, and adversarial concerns (2.6). The synthesis in Section 2.7
identifies the specific integration gap that the multilayered model is designed to address.
2.2 Theoretical Framework
2.2.1 Behavioural Biometrics Theory
Behavioural biometrics treats repeated human actions as measurable identity evidence. Latency
patterns produced while typing a known string can be compared with an enrolled reference to
authenticate identity [5]. The theoretical proposition relevant to this study is that timing
behaviour contains intra-user regularity and inter-user variation that can be represented
numerically.
The theory supports the selection of dwell time, flight time, and profile-centred deviations
because these variables operationalise typing rhythm [6], [5], [8]. Evidence can be collected
through ordinary keyboard events without requiring a physiological sensor [10], [20].
However, behavioural measurements vary within the same person because timing can be
affected by conditions such as fatigue [11] and input device [12]; consequently, a behavioural
template must be evaluated for both discrimination and stability.
2.2.2 Concept Drift Theory
Learning under concept drift occurs when the target relationship changes because of an
observable or hidden context [14]. Later work distinguishes abrupt, gradual, recurring, and
incremental change and shows that a model trained on historical observations may become less
reliable when the underlying distribution evolves [15].
Concept Drift Theory explains why a keystroke profile cannot be assumed to remain
permanently stable. Its strength is that it directs attention from initial model fit to detection,
adaptation, and recovery. Its limitation is that a statistical change signal does not by itself
17

identify the cause of change or determine whether the new behaviour is legitimate;
authentication policy and labelled feedback remain necessary.
2.2.3 Theoretical Synthesis
Behavioural Biometrics Theory explains why keystroke timing can distinguish users, while
Concept Drift Theory explains why that distinction may weaken over time. Together they
imply a model with two linked responsibilities: classify current behaviour relative to an
enrolled profile and monitor whether classification error indicates that the profile-model
relationship has changed.
2.3 Related Works
2.3.1 Continuous Authentication
Continuous authentication extends identity assurance beyond the entry-point decision by
collecting additional evidence while a session remains active [2], [3]. It does not replace login
authentication; instead, it addresses the different question of whether subsequent interaction
remains consistent with the authenticated user.
Continuous authentication can draw on behavioural signals across devices, but practical
systems must manage acquisition conditions, user variability, privacy, and response latency
[3]. Keystroke dynamics has been shown to support continuous verification [2], and
behavioural biometrics must be evaluated as security mechanisms rather than solely as pattern-
recognition exercises [21].
The literature therefore identifies two simultaneous requirements: security-oriented detection
of anomalous behaviour and usability-oriented tolerance of legitimate within-user variation [3],
[21], [20]. A continuous system must also define what happens after a low score, such as
reauthentication, warning, restricted access, or controlled model adaptation [1], [3], [13]. These
requirements motivate explicit FAR, FRR, threshold, and drift-recovery evaluation.
2.3.2 Keystroke Dynamics as Behavioural Biometrics
Keystroke dynamics derives behavioural features from recorded key-event timestamps. Dwell
time measures the duration of a key press, while flight or transition measures describe the
interval between successive events [6], [5], [8]. Fixed-text systems compare repeated instances
of the same password or phrase; free-text systems must compare variable language sequences
[22].
18

Typing timing has been shown to discriminate users under controlled protocols [5], [6], [7],
[19]. The signal can be collected from standard keyboard events, but the input device [12],
collection software, feature definitions, enrolment design, and decision protocol materially
affect the resulting evidence [10], [20].
The literature also identifies limitations and objections. Keystroke timing changes have been
observed under mental fatigue [11], and cross-device studies show that the input device can
affect authentication features and performance [12]. Practical problems include intra-user
variability, limited enrolment data, and operating-threshold selection [20], while reported
performance depends strongly on feature representation, dataset, classifier, and evaluation
protocol [10]. Imitation, replay, and unsafe adaptive updates create additional security concerns
[23], [24], [25]. These limitations support using keystroke dynamics as an additional
behavioural assurance signal rather than an infallible replacement for a strong primary
authenticator.
Despite these limitations, keystroke dynamics is appropriate for the present study because prior
work demonstrates identity information in sequential typing latencies [6], [5], [7], while
adaptive keystroke research demonstrates the need to manage behavioural change [13]. The
study therefore combines transparent timing features with explicit monitoring instead of
claiming that the modality is universally superior.
2.3.3 Concept Drift in Authentication
Concept drift occurs when the statistical relationship between predictor variables and the target
changes over time [14], [15]. In keystroke authentication, a shift may arise from legitimate
behavioural evolution [11], [13], an input-device change [12], or a different operator. The
security meaning cannot be inferred from the drift alarm alone; the alarm indicates that the
model's previous evidence relationship requires review.
2.3.4 Adaptive Stream Learning
Stream learners process observations sequentially and update model state without repeatedly
retraining on the complete historical dataset [26]-[31]. Hoeffding Trees support incremental
tree construction, while ensemble methods maintain multiple learners to improve robustness.
Streaming Random Patches combines random feature and sample subspaces with incremental
base learners, making it suitable for the controlled adaptation experiment.
19

2.4 Drift Detection Methods
Drift Detection Method (DDM) monitors the online error rate and its standard deviation and
signals warning or drift when error exceeds historical bounds [32]. Early Drift Detection
Method (EDDM) instead monitors the distance between classification errors and is intended to
improve sensitivity to gradual change [33]. Support-vector-based approaches detect changes in
decision structure but may require greater computational effort [34].
Adaptive Windowing (ADWIN) maintains a variable-length window and compares sub-
window means to detect statistically significant change [16]. Its main advantage is that it does
not require a fixed monitoring window. Its limitations are dependence on the delta sensitivity
parameter and the fact that it detects distributional change without explaining its cause. The
methodology selects ADWIN because it can monitor the binary prediction-error stream
independently of the classifier.
2.5 Biometric Performance Evaluation
Biometric authentication must report security and usability errors separately. FAR measures
impostor acceptance, whereas FRR measures genuine-user rejection [35], [36]. Accuracy alone
can hide uneven class behaviour, so balanced accuracy, confusion counts, and threshold-
sensitive measures are required [37]-[39]. AUC-ROC summarises ranking performance across
thresholds, while the selected operating threshold determines the observed FAR and FRR.
2.6 Security, Privacy, and Adversarial Concerns
Keystroke timing is biometric information and therefore requires purpose limitation, access
control, secure storage, and protection against linkage or replay [23]. Wider cybersecurity
research places biometrics and explainable artificial intelligence within defence-in-depth
practice [40]. Adversarial-learning literature also shows that predictive systems may be evaded
or poisoned when attackers can probe decisions or influence updates [24], [25]. These concerns
require adaptation to be controlled and logged rather than allowing every new sample to
redefine the enrolled profile.
2.7 Research Gap
The reviewed studies establish that keystroke timing can support authentication [5], [19],
continuous verification requires evidence beyond login [2], [3], and changing streams require
detection and adaptation [14], [15], [16]. However, these bodies of work are commonly
evaluated in isolation. Keystroke studies often end with a static benchmark score, while drift
20

studies evaluate generic streams without connecting the alarm to an authentication decision
and interpretable response.
The resulting gap is an integrated-evaluation gap: limited work demonstrates, in one
reproducible artifact, how profile-centred timing features, biometric classification, statistical
error monitoring, adaptive stream learning, threshold policy, and user-facing feedback operate
together as a cohesive authentication pipeline. Most keystroke studies report only static
benchmark performance, while most drift studies evaluate generic streams without connecting
detection to an authentication decision. Furthermore, security and adversarial concerns
including poisoning, mimicry, and template protection are rarely evaluated alongside
biometric performance within a single study. The literature therefore compels a study that
integrates these components and evaluates them not as isolated contributions but as a single
multilayered authentication artifact. The present study addresses that gap through a
multilayered model evaluated by benchmark discrimination and controlled post-drift resilience.
It does not claim geographic generalisability or production readiness.
2.8 Chapter Summary
Behavioural Biometrics Theory supports the use of keystroke timing as identity evidence, while
Concept Drift Theory establishes why a model based on that evidence requires continued
monitoring. Prior work demonstrates useful discrimination but also reports within-user
variability, protocol dependence, privacy risk, and vulnerability to changing conditions. The
literature therefore supports an integrated model whose evaluation includes FAR, FRR, AUC-
ROC, drift detection, and recovery. Chapter 3 describes how that model was developed and
tested.
21

CHAPTER 3: RESEARCH METHODOLOGY
3.1 Introduction
This chapter presents the methodology used to conduct the study. It explains the research
design, data sources, feature engineering approach, model evaluation protocols, validity
considerations, and ethical boundaries. The chapter focuses on research method and evaluation
logic rather than implementation code.
3.2 Research Design
The study used a quantitative design-science research design. Design Science Research
structured the construction and evaluation of the authentication artifact [17], [18], while
quantitative experiments measured classification performance and controlled drift response.
The design was appropriate because the research questions required both development of a
model and numerical evaluation of its discrimination, monitoring, and recovery behaviour.
3.3 Design Science Research Methodology
Design Science Research (DSR) was used as the research methodology because the study
developed and evaluated an information-system artifact [17], [18]. The DSR activities
comprised problem identification, definition of objectives, design and development,
demonstration, evaluation, and communication. These activities guided the work; DSR is not
described here as a software-development process.
The artifact consisted of a feature-processing component, a benchmark authentication
classifier, an adaptive stream classifier, an ADWIN error watchdog, an exported model artifact,
and a dashboard demonstration. Quantitative experiments evaluated whether these components
met the research objectives.

3.4 Data Sources
3.4.1 CMU DSL Strong Password Benchmark
The original CMU DSL Strong Password dataset contains 20,400 fixed-text samples collected
from 51 subjects. Each observation includes three identifier columns (subject code, session
index, repetition index) and 31 timing variables: 11 key-hold (dwell) features, 10 key-down-
to-key-down latency features, and 10 key-up-to-key-down (flight) latency features [19]. Each
subject typed the password phrase 400 times across eight sessions, with 50 repetitions per
session and at least one day between consecutive sessions [19]. The data contain three identifier
columns and 31 timing variables: 11 hold-time features, 10 key-down-to-key-down latencies,
and 10 key-up-to-key-down latencies.
The study sorted observations by subject, session, and repetition. Hold-time columns were
averaged per sample and converted to milliseconds to obtain dwell timing; key-up-to-key-down
columns were averaged and converted to milliseconds to obtain flight timing. Subject s036 was
23

used as the enrolled genuine user in the defined one-versus-rest deployment experiment, while
all other subjects supplied impostor samples.
3.4.2 Synthetic Stream for Drift Evaluation
A deterministic synthetic stream of 10,000 observations was generated with random seed 42.
Each observation was labelled genuine with probability 0.80 and impostor with probability
0.20. Before drift, genuine dwell times followed a Gaussian distribution with mean 105 ms and
standard deviation 16 ms, and genuine flight times used mean 72 ms and standard deviation 12
ms. Impostor observations used dwell mean 145 ms (SD 28 ms) and flight mean 98 ms (SD 20
ms).
Abrupt drift was introduced at observation 2,500. For genuine samples after that point, dwell
mean increased by 18 ms, flight mean increased by 30 ms, and flight-time variability was
multiplied by 1.4. Values were bounded below at 20 ms for dwell and 10 ms for flight. These
settings produced a known change point against which ADWIN detection and model recovery
could be examined.
The synthetic design is an experimental mechanism, not evidence of natural human drift. Its
methodological basis is the concept-drift requirement for distinguishable pre-change and post-
change distributions [14], [15]. Empirical keystroke studies show that fatigue, device, and
behavioural adaptation can produce real variation [11], [12], [13]; therefore, the synthetic
stream permits repeatable mechanism testing but does not replace longitudinal human
validation.
3.5 Population, Census, and Unit of Analysis
The benchmark population comprised all 51 subjects and all 20,400 observations in the CMU
dataset; therefore, no sample of subjects was drawn and the dataset was treated as a census of
the available benchmark. Within the deployment protocol, subject s036 supplied 200 training
and 200 testing observations. Each of the other 50 subjects supplied five training and five
testing impostor observations, giving 450 training and 450 testing samples.
The unit of analysis was one fixed-text typing sample represented by timing measurements.
The synthetic experiment used generated observations rather than a human population; its unit
of analysis was one labelled dwell-flight observation in the stream.
24

3.6 Data Preparation and Feature Engineering
3.6.1 Data Preparation
The original data were sorted by subject, session index, and repetition to preserve collection
order. Identifier columns were retained for protocol construction but excluded from model
predictors. Genuine and impostor subsets were separated before baseline calculation. Training
statistics were calculated from the training partition only, preventing test information from
entering the scaler or enrolled profile.
3.6.2 Feature Engineering
For each sample, dwell_ms was calculated as the mean of the 11 hold-time columns multiplied
by 1,000. flight_ms was calculated as the mean of the 10 key-up-to-key-down latency columns
multiplied by 1,000. The genuine training profile was defined by baseline dwell of 44.625 ms
and baseline flight of 559.284 ms.
Two model predictors were then calculated: dwell_delta = |dwell_ms - baseline_dwell| and
flight_delta = |flight_ms - baseline_flight|. These profile-centred variables measure how far the
current sample lies from the enrolled user's training profile. Training-set means and standard
deviations standardised both predictors before logistic-regression fitting.
3.7 Model Development
The deployment classifier was logistic regression with class_weight="balanced",
random_state=42, and max_iter=500. The model received the two standardised profile-centred
predictors and estimated the probability of the genuine class. Class balancing compensated for
the unequal construction of genuine and impostor training observations.
A parameter-selection audit compared C values 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 with and without
balanced class weighting using five-fold stratified cross-validation on the s036 training
partition. The best mean balanced accuracy was 0.9895 (SD 0.0072) at C=10 without class
weighting. The deployed C=1 balanced model was retained as the documented browser artifact
because it was already integrated and achieved comparable high validation performance; the
audit is reported as a sensitivity check rather than a post-hoc replacement based on test results.
The classifier was fitted on 450 observations. Thresholds from 0.3000 to 0.9500 were evaluated
in 0.0025 increments, and the threshold that maximised balanced accuracy was retained. The
selected threshold was 0.5875. The fitted coefficients were -6.1080 for dwell_delta and -0.2853
25

for flight_delta, with intercept -2.6676; therefore, larger timing deviations reduced the
estimated probability of genuine behaviour.
The stream model was a Streaming Random Patches classifier with 12 Hoeffding Tree base
learners, grace_period=100, and seed 42. A Min-Max scaler updated online. ADWIN used
delta=0.002 and monitored binary prediction error. On drift detection, the experiment recorded
an event and reinitialised the stream ensemble and detector with a deterministic updated seed.
3.8 Drift Simulation Design
The drift experiment used the distributions defined in Section 3.4.2 and a prequential test-then-
train sequence. Each observation was transformed, predicted, compared with its true label, and
passed to the accuracy metric and ADWIN detector before the classifier learned from it. This
order prevents the model from learning an observation before being evaluated on it.
Resilience was evaluated through the final prequential accuracy, number of detected events,
and recovery position. Recovery was defined as the first post-detection sample at which
cumulative accuracy reached at least 0.80. Because cumulative accuracy can conceal short-
term variation, the interpretation is limited to the controlled experiment and its explicit
recovery rule.
3.9 Evaluation Protocols
3.9.1 Benchmark Protocol
The benchmark protocol used 200 genuine training observations and 200 genuine testing
observations from subject s036. For each of the 50 remaining subjects, the first five
observations supplied impostor training data and the next five supplied impostor testing data.
Baseline and scaling statistics were calculated only from the training partition.
A secondary subject-wide analysis repeated the same split for each of all 51 subjects. Logistic-
regression parameters were selected by five-fold cross-validation on the s036 training partition,
and each subject-specific operating threshold was selected from five-fold out-of-fold
probabilities on that subject's training partition. The untouched test partition then provided
accuracy, balanced accuracy, AUC-ROC, FAR, FRR, precision, recall, F1, and EER.
Aggregate means and normal-approximation 95% confidence intervals summarised between-
subject performance.
26

3.9.2 Streaming Protocol
The streaming protocol used 10,000 generated observations, drift at index 2,500, and ADWIN
delta 0.002. Prediction preceded learning for every observation. The same fixed seed and
parameters were used for the reported run in the executed jonga_thesis_model.ipynb notebook.
3.10 Evaluation Metrics
Accuracy measured the proportion of correct decisions, while balanced accuracy averaged
genuine recall and impostor recall. FAR measured FP/(FP+TN), and FRR measured
FN/(FN+TP). Precision, recall, and F1 were calculated for the genuine class. AUC-ROC
measured probability-ranking performance across all thresholds [37]-[39]. The confusion
matrix reported TP, TN, FP, and FN.
Equal-error rate (EER) was estimated at the ROC point where FAR and FRR were closest.
Lower EER indicates a better overall biometric trade-off. For subject-wide means, the 95%
confidence interval was calculated as the mean plus or minus 1.96 multiplied by the standard
error across 51 subjects.
Stream evaluation reported final prequential accuracy, detected drift-event count, and recovery
sample index. These measures correspond respectively to overall online performance,
watchdog response, and adaptation after the known change point.
3.11 Quality Assurance Framework
Quality assurance was implemented through fixed random seed 42, deterministic ordering,
explicit train-test counts, training-only baseline and scaling statistics, a recorded threshold
search range, and export of feature order, coefficients, scaler values, protocol metadata, counts,
and metrics to keystroke_model.json. The executed jonga_thesis_model.ipynb notebook

4.3 Model Layer Design
4.3.1 Layer 1: Feature Processing Design
The feature-processing layer converts raw keystroke timestamps into compact behavioural
variables. For the deployed benchmark model, the average hold-time features in the dataset are
converted into dwell milliseconds, while key transition timing features are converted into flight
milliseconds. A genuine baseline profile is then calculated from the training samples.
Each new sample is represented by its absolute distance from the genuine baseline. This design
makes the model interpretable: close timing deltas suggest normal behaviour, while larger
deltas indicate possible impostor behaviour or drift.
At a conceptual level, the layer treats keyboard timing as an information-bearing signal: the
typed password supplies symbolic content, while the timing sequence supplies behavioural
evidence. This distinction follows the broader information-theoretic idea that communication
events can carry measurable structure beyond their visible symbols [43].

4.5 Drift Watchdog Design
The drift watchdog is designed around prediction error rather than raw timing alone. Raw
dwell-time or flight-time changes may reflect ordinary variation, but they become operationally
important when they damage authentication reliability. For this reason, each stream sample is
first transformed into timing features, predicted by the stream classifier, and then compared
with the true label. The result is an error stream where zero represents a correct prediction and
one represents a wrong prediction.

Figure 4.4: ADWIN drift-watchdog operation.
Figure 4.4 presents the prequential error stream, ADWIN decision, normal update path, reset

ADWIN monitors this error stream using an adaptive window. When the error distribution
remains stable, the classifier continues the normal test-then-train loop and learns from the
current sample. When ADWIN signals sustained change, the prototype treats this as model-
health degradation, increments the drift-event count, reinitialises the Streaming Random

hook that makes the resilience mechanism transparent for academic demonstration.
The watchdog is separated from the classifier so that model learning and model-health
monitoring remain modular. Future versions could compare ADWIN [16] with DDM [32],
EDDM [33], or SVM-based drift detection [34], or replace reset behaviour with warm-start
retraining, ensemble-member replacement, sliding-window retraining, or confidence-weighted
adaptation. The prototype also records recovery evidence, including running accuracy after
drift, the first recovery index, and the number of detected drift events.

4.6.1 Authentication Decision Logic
The authentication decision is not based on password text alone. The dashboard first checks
whether the password condition is satisfied, then compares the current typing rhythm with the
enrolled behavioural profile. This creates a layered decision: possession of the secret is
necessary but not sufficient when the timing pattern is inconsistent.
In the deployment model, the current dwell and flight timings are converted into deltas against
the baseline profile. These deltas are normalized using exported training statistics. The logistic
function then produces a probability-like score. The score is compared with the tuned threshold
to determine whether the timing behaviour is accepted.
This design is explainable because an access denial can be tied to timing deviation. The
interface can show whether dwell time, flight time, or both moved away from the baseline,
supporting the dissertation's emphasis on decision support rather than opaque scoring.

The threshold search examined values from 0.3000 to 0.9500 and selected 0.5875 because it

more difficult and may reduce false acceptance at the cost of higher false rejection. Lowering
it would have the opposite effect. The selected value is therefore an empirical operating point

CHAPTER 6: CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS
6.1 Summary of Findings
Profile-centred dwell and flight deviations supported strong discrimination for subject s036:
accuracy was 0.9956, balanced accuracy 0.9960, AUC-ROC 0.99956, FAR 0.0080, and FRR
0.0000. The subject-wide analysis was more moderate, with mean balanced accuracy 0.7708,
mean AUC-ROC 0.8315, and mean EER 0.2274. In the synthetic stream, final prequential
accuracy was 0.8700, ADWIN detected one event, and the defined recovery level was reached
at sample 2,529.
6.2 Conclusions Against the Objectives
For Objective 1, the study concludes that the two profile-centred timing features had high
discriminative power for the selected s036 fixed-text case but variable effectiveness across
users. The 51-subject analysis therefore supports cautious, user-specific calibration rather than
a universal performance claim.
For Objective 2, the study concludes that drift detection can be incorporated as a separate error-
monitoring layer coupled to an adaptive stream classifier. This separation allows the classifier
to make predictions while ADWIN independently monitors whether error behaviour has
changed.
For Objective 3, the study concludes that the implemented model was resilient to the specific
abrupt synthetic change defined in the methodology because the event was detected and the
recovery criterion was reached. The conclusion is limited to controlled synthetic drift and does
not claim proven resilience to natural longitudinal typing change.
6.3 Recommendations
Future researchers should extend the completed 51-subject benchmark with nested parameter
selection, independent threshold-calibration sets, repeated cross-validation, and per-user
confidence intervals. Longitudinal fixed-text and free-text data should also be collected across
devices and sessions because prior studies demonstrate fatigue-related [11], device-related
[12], and adaptation-related variation [13].
System developers extending the prototype should calibrate thresholds per user [20], protect
biometric templates [23], restrict and audit adaptive updates [13], test mimicry and poisoning
attacks [24], [25], and combine keystroke evidence with a strong primary authenticator rather
than using it as a replacement.
50

Institutions considering behavioural authentication should first conduct a privacy and security
assessment, define reauthentication and appeal procedures, measure latency and resource use,
and perform a user study before operational deployment, consistent with identity-lifecycle and
biometric-information protection guidance [1], [23].
6.4 Practical Implications
The implementation demonstrates that a compact model can be exported to a browser and
accompanied by visible threshold and drift information. For security teams, the important
implication is that model monitoring must be planned together with model deployment. For
users, the observed zero FRR is encouraging for the selected protocol, but broader testing is
required before drawing usability conclusions.
6.5 Contribution to Knowledge
The study contributes an evaluated integration of behavioural-biometric classification and
concept-drift monitoring. The identity value of keystroke latency was established early on [5],
while the learning problem created by changing contexts was shown later [14]. This
dissertation connects those foundations in a reproducible authentication artifact whose outputs

The contribution is not a new drift algorithm or a universal authentication model. It is the design
